title: An AI-Driven, Player-Expanding Dark Fantasy MUD
author: Least-Monk-131
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m a software developer working on a passion project that sits at the intersection of old-school text adventures and modern AI. I wanted to share a bit about the architecture I’m building for Homeris, a Dark Fantasy MUD.

I've always loved the depth of MUDs, but I wanted to make the experience more accessible and immersive for 2026. Here is the technical breakdown of what I’m working on:

The Stack: I’m building a custom backend in Java/Netty from the ground up to ensure low latency. The world state is persisted using a PostgreSQL database, managed via a Docker environment.

The "Interactive Audiobook" Mode: I realized that reading walls of text can be a barrier. I’ve integrated a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline that takes the room description, NPC memories (stored in NPC\_CHRONICLES), and player state, and feeds it to an LLM to generate a dynamic, narrative-focused audio experience.

Persistent & Living NPCs: NPCs in Homeris aren't static scripts. They use a Utility-based AI Brain to decide their actions based on personality traits, and they actually remember their own history, which they can recount during interactions.

I’m currently in the "building in public" phase, documenting the technical hurdles and the code behind the integration of LLMs into a persistent world.

If you’re interested in the code, the technical challenges of running persistent AI-driven worlds, or just want to follow the progress, I’m posting my DevLogs here: \[Link al tuo Patreon\]

I’d love to hear your thoughts on how you’re handling LLM integration in your projects, or any feedback on the concept!

comments.author: soulfir
comments.body: The thing that will bite you around month two is memory contradiction, not memory loss. An NPC will remember selling you a sword and, separately, remember never meeting you, because each memory gets generated fresh against slightly different context and your retrieval will surface both as equally true. The high-level lesson, and it cost me a while to learn: the model is great at recall-flavored prose and bad at being the actual record of what happened. The more you keep the canonical facts as something the model only reads from, rather than something it regenerates each turn, the longer the illusion holds. Looks like a strong project so far.

replies.author: Least-Monk-131
replies.body:
Spot on! *'Great at recall-flavored prose and bad at being the actual record'* is probably the most accurate way to frame this problem.

You hit the exact technical nerve I've been focusing on. Relying on the LLM to dynamically regenerate or maintain the historical record is a recipe for broken immersion. That's precisely why I separated the architecture from day one.

In Homeris, the 'canonical facts' (inventories, quest states, world events, and major NPC relationship flags) live strictly inside a rigid PostgreSQL database. The RAG pipeline's job isn't to let the AI guess or regenerate what happened, but to fetch those deterministic SQL facts and use the LLM purely as a narrative wrapper.

Basically, Postgres dictates *what* happened, and the LLM only decides *how* to tell the story based on the NPC's profile.

Thanks for the solid feedback, insights like yours are exactly why I decided to build this in public!

replies.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
replies.body:
I have a similar project, you need something like sleeping in humans.  It's sort of counterintuitive but memories need to be allowed to fade, reorganize and change. 

Will this ultimately run on local models? Have you chosen a model yet? Very important to choose at least a family of models. Otherwise you're trying to tune a model-agnostic prompt which is a recipe for frustration.

replies.author: Least-Monk-131
replies.body:
That’s a fascinating perspective! The concept of a 'sleep cycle' for data reorganization and consolidation is actually something I’m looking into. Allowing minor memories to compress, fade, or merge into broader behavioral traits (instead of keeping thousands of raw text chunks forever) is a great way to prevent context bloat and keep token usage efficient.

To answer your questions:

**1. Local Models:** Yes, absolutely. The ultimate goal is to run everything locally on a dedicated home server (a Debian Mini PC environment with a dedicated GPU pipeline). Privacy, zero API costs, and total control over response times are non-negotiable for a project like this.

**2. Model Choice & Prompting:** You hit the nail on the head regarding model-agnostic prompts. It's a recipe for madness. Right now, in the development/testing phase, I'm leaning heavily towards the **Llama 3** family (specifically tuning for the 8B and 70B variants depending on the task's complexity, like quick actions vs deep lore generation) and looking closely at **Mistral** alternatives.

I’m structuring the Java backend to handle model-specific formatting layers so that the system behavior remains tightly controlled around the target family’s strengths.

Are you running your project on local hardware as well? What family did you settle on?

replies.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
replies.body:
No, I'm running on cloud models, specifically gemini. I tried local for quite awhile but ultimately wanted the barrier to entry for my game to be low and just couldn't find a solid way of doing that locally.  Most of my player play on mobile, so I'm glad I did.  Being at the mercy of google kind of sucks though. 

I'd encourage you to start with small models and only go bigger when you absolutely need to.  Otherwise the strength of the model hides some of the weaknesses of your system.

replies.author: Least-Monk-131
replies.body:
That makes total sense, especially when targeting mobile players where seamless scalability is key. Being at the mercy of big tech APIs is definitely the tough trade-off there.

Your advice about starting with smaller models is absolute gold, and it actually aligns perfectly with my current setup. Right now, I'm benchmarking several different models using **Ollama** as my local engine. My immediate goal is to make everything run efficiently on a local Mini PC. Since this hardware obviously isn't powerful enough to handle massive, ultra-complex models, I *have* to focus heavily on tuning the system against smaller and simpler variants (like the 8B models).

You are so right—a powerful cloud model can easily mask a poorly optimized prompt or a messy context payload because it's 'smart' enough to patch the holes. If I can get the RAG orchestration, entity states, and context structuring to deliver a great, coherent experience on a smaller local model due to my hardware constraints, I’ll know the underlying Java framework and database schema are truly rock solid.

Thanks for sharing your experience, it's really reassuring to discuss these architectural crossroads with someone building in the same space!
